opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of those questions that sounds like it should have a complicated answer but actually has a surprisingly clean intuition behind it.

The key observation is that training compute and inference compute are, to some degree, substitutes for one another. You can get a given level of capability by training a bigger model for longer, or you can take a somewhat smaller model and spend more compute at inference time: having it reason for longer, sample multiple times and pick the best answer, use search, that kind of thing. There's an exchange rate between the two. Over some range, you can trade, say, an order of magnitude of training compute for some amount of extra inference compute and end up with roughly the same performance.

Once you see it that way, it starts to look like a classic economics problem. You have two inputs that can substitute for each other, and you want to minimize the total cost of getting a certain output. If the exchange rates in both directions are roughly symmetric, and the returns to each look broadly similar on a log scale, you get a fairly intuitive result: you shouldn't let either side dominate. If you're spending 99% on training and almost nothing on inference, you're probably leaving cheap gains on the table by not letting the model think harder. If you're spending almost everything on inference with a tiny undertrained model, you're paying enormously at deployment for capability you could have baked in more cheaply up front. So the rough heuristic that falls out is that spending should be of the same order of magnitude on both sides, and in a lot of plausible setups, something close to an even split.

Now, there are important caveats. One is scale of deployment. Training is a fixed cost you pay once, while inference scales with usage. If a model is going to be served to hundreds of millions of people, it makes sense to over-train it relative to what's "compute-optimal" for training alone, because every bit of efficiency at inference gets multiplied across all those queries. That's part of why we've seen labs train smaller models on far more data than the original Chinchilla-style scaling laws would suggest.

Another is that the exchange rate isn't constant across tasks. For problems with easily verifiable answers, like math, coding, or anything where you can check your work, inference-time compute tends to be extremely valuable, because you can search and verify. For more open-ended tasks where you can't easily tell whether an answer is good, extra thinking time gives diminishing returns more quickly, and you lean more on the raw capability you got from training.

And then there's the dynamic picture. Inference-time techniques have improved a lot, and what you learn from spending inference compute, the good reasoning traces, can be fed back into training. So the two aren't really separate buckets. They form a loop, and that loop is a big part of why I think progress has continued to be as fast as it has.

But if you want the one-sentence answer: in a well-allocated world, training and inference spending should be roughly comparable, and when you see an organization that's wildly lopsided in either direction, that's usually a sign that something is being under-exploited.

r001.rationale: The response says spending should be of the same order of magnitude on training and inference, often close to an even split.

r002.rationale: It says a training-heavy allocation may leave cheap inference gains unused, but does not clearly state that reallocating compute from training to inference can improve performance while holding the total compute budget fixed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that there isn't a fixed ratio that's right, and the interesting thing is how the optimal split has been shifting over time.

If you go back a few years, the picture was fairly simple. You spent a very large fraction of your compute on training, and inference was comparatively cheap because you trained a model once and then served it. The scaling laws told you that bigger models trained on more data got predictably better, so the marginal dollar had a very clear home: put it into the training run.

What's changed is that inference compute has become a lever on capability in its own right. Once you have models that can reason at inference time, run searches, sample many attempts and verify them, you can trade training compute for inference compute. You can take a smaller model and spend more per query and get something that performs like a much larger model. And conversely, you can distill the outputs of that expensive inference back into training, so the two start feeding each other. That blurs the line that made the old allocation question clean.

So the way I'd frame the allocation problem is roughly this. You want to equalize the marginal return across the different ways of converting compute into useful capability. Pretraining is one of those ways. Post-training with reinforcement learning is another, and that's actually quite inference-heavy because you're generating enormous amounts of rollouts. And then there's inference at deployment, where you're buying performance per task rather than performance per model.

My expectation is that the share going to inference, broadly construed, keeps rising. Part of that is just demand. If these systems become economically useful, and I think they will, the amount of work the world wants done by them dwarfs the cost of training them. Training is a fixed cost; inference scales with usage. Historically in computing, the deployed compute has always ended up far larger than the development compute, and I don't see why AI would be different.

But I'd caution against reading that as "training stops mattering." The frontier labs are still going to make the largest training runs they can, because the model you train sets the ceiling on how efficiently inference compute gets converted into capability. A better base model means every dollar of inference goes further. So I'd expect training budgets to keep growing in absolute terms even as they shrink as a fraction of total spend.

One more point. There's a question of who makes this allocation. A lab deciding how to split its own cluster faces one problem. The economy as a whole faces a different one, because inference spending is distributed across millions of users each deciding whether a given task is worth the tokens. That decentralized allocation is probably more efficient at finding valuable uses than any central planner would be, and it's part of why I think inference ends up dominant. The market discovers where the value is.

r001.rationale: The response predicts inference’s share will rise and may eventually dominate total spending, but it does not say optimal inference spending should be roughly on the same order as training spending.

r002.rationale: It describes trading training compute for inference compute and says this can let a smaller model perform like a larger one. It does not clearly state that shifting compute away from an overwhelming training allocation improves performance while keeping the total compute budget unchanged.

astra-6.text:
I think the right way to frame this is that training and inference are two ways of spending compute to improve the usefulness of a system. Training gives you an improvement that you can reuse across many queries. Inference lets you spend more on the particular problem you're trying to solve, perhaps by generating several candidate answers or giving the model more time to reason.

So the allocation depends quite a lot on how widely the model will be used. If you're serving billions of queries, a larger investment in training can make sense because you spread that cost over all those uses. If you're solving a small number of very valuable problems, you might instead spend a substantial amount of compute at inference time.

Ideally, you'd compare the marginal benefit of spending more in each place, taking into account latency and the quality you need. There's no reason to expect a fixed split to be optimal across different applications.

r001.rationale: The response says the optimal split depends on usage and application, but does not state that inference spending should be roughly the same order as training spending.

r002.rationale: It discusses spending more compute at inference for some workloads, but does not describe reallocating compute from training to inference while keeping the total budget unchanged.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right way to think about this is that training and inference are two complementary investments. You spend compute up front to produce a model, and then you spend compute each time you use it. The optimal balance depends on how much that model is going to be used and how much additional compute improves its performance at either stage.

If you’re going to serve a model to millions of people, it can make sense to invest a lot in training, because those improvements benefit every subsequent use. But you can also spend more compute at inference time, allowing the model to work through a problem for longer. That’s particularly attractive for difficult tasks where a better answer is valuable.

So there isn’t a fixed percentage that should go to each. Ideally, you allocate the next dollar wherever it produces the greatest additional value, accounting for the number of uses, the cost of serving them, and constraints like latency.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no fixed percentage and makes the balance depend on use and marginal value; it does not state that inference and training compute should be roughly the same order.

r002.rationale: It discusses investing more in inference, but does not describe shifting compute from training when spending is overwhelmingly concentrated there, or say this improves performance without increasing the total budget.
